video_title: Mark Skousen: Why He's Still 100% Invested at All-Time Highs
gist: Economist and newsletter writer Mark Skousen argues the US is in a technology-led 'golden era' with record corporate profits and B2B supply-chain spending growing faster than GDP, so he stays 100% invested at all-time highs while treating inflation as a permanent, policy-driven regime that forces investors to compound 8-10% a year just to break even. His portfolio answer is diversification across dividend-paying financials and energy, miners and royalty companies over physical commodities, copper/uranium/blockchain equities, and zero bonds, with a pre-defined exit trigger: hedge-fund or private-equity bankruptcies that start to spread. He simultaneously warns the $40 trillion debt, $2 trillion deficit and $7 trillion of Treasury refinancing mean the US will 'hit a wall,' and calls Bessent's Treasury buybacks a short-term fool's errand.

themes.theme: Gross output vs GDP: the bull case for the economy

insights.claim: Mark Skousen argues GDP understates the economy because it omits the business-to-business supply chain, which by his gross output measure is larger than GDP itself.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Investors tracking only GDP miss the B2B capex cycle; gross output can flag industrial and supplier earnings turns before consumer data does.
insights.quote: GDP leaves out the supply chain, which is bigger than GDP itself

insights.claim: Business-to-business spending is now growing faster than GDP after two years of tariff- and pandemic-driven supply chain strain, which Skousen reads as business finally catching up to the consumer.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A B2B-led acceleration favors industrials, distributors and suppliers over consumer-facing names in the next leg.

insights.claim: Corporate profits are at record highs and the bears are ignoring that, according to Skousen, who says repeated predictions of economic collapse have not materialized.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Earnings support for the all-time-high market is fundamental, not purely multiple expansion, which weakens the simple 'it's all a bubble' short case.

insights.claim: The AI technology boom is driving productivity and the stock market to records but has not helped the labor market, leaving employment and general economic growth sluggish.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A market that rises on productivity while jobs stay weak keeps political pressure on the Fed to cut even as market rates rise, a persistent policy tension to trade around.

themes.theme: Permanent inflation as policy, not cycle

insights.claim: Skousen frames US inflation as a permanent policy regime rather than a cyclical event, because the Federal Reserve abandoned price stability for Bernanke's 2% target while the country runs fiat money and large deficits.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: If inflation is structural policy, cash and fixed-rate bonds are a permanent tax and real-asset exposure is a baseline allocation, not a hedge.
insights.quote: We have a permanent inflation policy. That is our policy.

insights.claim: Skousen says the post-World War II price level looks like a hockey stick that has never come back down, in contrast to the first 200 years of US history when prices rose and fell.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Mean-reversion assumptions about consumer prices are historically wrong post-1945; portfolios should be built for a one-way price level.

insights.claim: Investors need net worth growth of roughly 8 to 10 percent a year simply to stay ahead of structural inflation, per Skousen's hurdle rate.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: That hurdle rules out most cash and investment-grade bond allocations and forces equity/real-asset weighting for anyone trying to preserve purchasing power.
insights.quote: you need to see an increase in your net worth by I think 8 to 10% a year just to stay ahead of this whole inflation problem

insights.claim: Skousen points to gold, Bitcoin, copper at all-time highs and rising uranium prices as broad evidence that inflation is showing up across commodities, not just groceries and gasoline.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Broad commodity strength argues the move is monetary rather than a single-commodity squeeze, supporting a basket approach over single-name commodity bets.

insights.claim: Skousen says Trump and the Republicans are in denial about inflation, a political blind spot he ties to the coming midterm elections.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: If inflation stays a live grievance into November, midterm outcomes and subsequent policy risk become a tradeable macro event.

themes.theme: Warsh's Fed and the rate path around the midterms

insights.claim: Skousen expects Kevin Warsh to postpone rate hikes as long as possible ahead of the midterm elections, with all bets off afterward if inflation persists.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Positions that depend on easy policy have a defined shelf life: the window closes after November, making post-midterm rate risk the key calendar trade.
insights.quote: I think he's going to postpone as long as possible the raising of rates, but all bets are off after the midterms.

insights.claim: Skousen argues the market is already telling the Fed to raise rates because market rates are rising, so Trump's demand for lower rates cannot be delivered.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Betting on Fed-driven lower long rates fights the market; duration exposure stays unattractive regardless of political pressure.

insights.claim: Skousen is optimistic on Kevin Warsh because Warsh models himself on Paul Volcker and has returned to watching the money supply, which Jerome Powell explicitly stopped doing.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A money-supply-watching Fed chair raises the odds of tighter-than-expected policy after the midterms, a risk for long-duration and speculative assets.

insights.claim: Skousen blames the 2020s inflation on a 40 percent money supply increase in a couple of years that Powell allowed by overreacting to the pandemic, with 2022 as the correction phase.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A monetarist read means money supply data, not labor prints, is the leading indicator for the next inflation impulse.

themes.theme: Fiscal wall and Treasury market plumbing

insights.claim: The US Treasury has to refinance $7 trillion this year, and Skousen warns foreign governments could choose gold, Bitcoin or Swiss francs over Treasuries at the margin.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Refinancing scale plus reserve-asset substitution is the mechanism for a rate spike; watch auction tails and official-sector gold buying as the tell.
insights.quote: the Treasury has to refinance $7 trillion this year

insights.claim: Skousen calls Scott Bessent's Treasury buyback program a short-term fool's errand aimed at holding rates artificially low through the midterms, and says it is not working because rates keep rising.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: If buybacks are failing, the rate suppression trade unwinds and long-end yields drift higher; it also removes a support many equity bulls are counting on.

insights.claim: Skousen says a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficit at full employment violates even Keynesian doctrine, which prescribes surpluses at full employment.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Running a deficit this size with no slack leaves no fiscal room for the next downturn, raising the probability the next crisis is met with monetization.
insights.quote: when you're at full employment you should be running a surplus not a $2 trillion deficit

insights.claim: Skousen uses Buchanan and Tullock's public choice theory to argue deficits are structurally inevitable because spending programs are popular with individual congressmen while taxes are not.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Treat fiscal consolidation as a low-probability scenario when pricing long bonds and inflation hedges; the incentive structure, not the personnel, drives deficits.

insights.claim: Skousen says the last period of US fiscal responsibility was the Clinton-Gingrich era of the late 1990s, and that 9/11, subsequent wars and expanded entitlements ended it.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Historical base rate: surpluses required divided government plus a boom, a combination not currently in place.

insights.claim: Skousen argues structural reform of Social Security and Medicare is unavoidable, citing Singapore's partially privatized Medisave system where healthcare is 5 percent of GDP versus 18 percent in the US.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A 13-point-of-GDP gap defines the size of the eventual US healthcare cost reset, a long-dated risk for managed care and hospital revenue models.

themes.theme: Yen carry trade and the next black swan

insights.claim: Skousen identifies the yen-dollar carry trade as a live black swan candidate: institutions borrowed yen at around 1 percent to buy US Treasuries yielding 4 to 5 percent, and must repay in a yen that has been dropping sharply.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Yen strength is the trigger to watch; a sharp reversal forces deleveraging of Treasury and risk-asset positions simultaneously.

insights.claim: Skousen says Scott Bessent intervened by buying Japanese yen specifically to keep private equity firms exposed to the carry trade from going under, an echo of Long-Term Capital Management in 1998.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Official intervention confirms the leverage is systemic; the size of that intervention is a proxy for how stressed the carry trade actually is.

insights.claim: Skousen's specific exit trigger for cutting equity exposure is hedge funds and private equity firms declaring bankruptcy in a way that starts to spread quickly, the Lehman Brothers pattern of 2008.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable de-risking signal: monitor credit events at levered financial intermediaries rather than equity drawdowns alone.

insights.claim: Skousen argues bringing inflation down is very difficult without bursting bubbles such as the carry trade, so disinflation itself is the risk event.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Successful Fed tightening is not a benign outcome for risk assets; positioning for disinflation should include tail hedges on levered credit.

insights.claim: Skousen says that even in a crisis he will not exit the market entirely but will raise cash and stay in income-producing stocks, invoking Richard Russell's rule that in a bear market the winner is the one who loses the least.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic bear-market objective: relative loss minimization via dividend cushion plus partial cash, not market timing.
insights.quote: in a bare market the winner is he who loses the least

insights.claim: Skousen is fully invested with only some cash reserved for special situations, and justifies it by saying modern liquidity lets him exit equities instantly with the click of a button.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: The whole position depends on liquidity being available at the moment of stress, historically the assumption that fails first in a crisis.
insights.quote: because we can get out of equities at any time with the click of a button, my dear

insights.claim: Skousen refuses to act on dated crash calls such as a predicted 2027 market massacre, saying he will wait until the market is actually and materially falling before reducing exposure.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A trend-following discipline that trades calendar-based doom forecasts for confirmation risk: he accepts being late in exchange for not being early.

insights.claim: Skousen applies Humphrey Neill's contrary-opinion rule that the public is right during trends but wrong at both ends, and notes those turning points occur only about once every ten years.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Because reversals are rare, fading the crowd mid-trend is a losing strategy; contrarianism only pays at extremes like 1999 and March 2009.
insights.quote: the public is right during the trends but wrong at both ends

insights.claim: Skousen says the market is in roughly the third year of a bull market in which every negative event produces a brief dip followed by new all-time highs, evidence to him that the market wants to go up.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Dip-buying persistence is the operative regime until a credit event breaks it; sell-the-rally strategies have been structurally penalized.

insights.claim: Skousen runs a deliberate benchmarking experiment: half his money in an S&P 500 index fund and half in individual stocks, ETFs and special situations, comparing the two every month and year.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A cheap, self-honest way to test whether active selection is adding value; investors who cannot beat the passive half should default to indexing.

insights.claim: Skousen holds no bond positions at all because rising rates mean falling bond prices, and substitutes dividend-paying stocks with rising dividend policies that yield more than Treasuries and bank CDs.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: An explicit rejection of the 60/40 model: the income sleeve moves from duration to equity dividend growth, with equity beta as the trade-off.

insights.claim: Skousen's income names span financials and energy: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Main Street Capital at about 7 percent, Enterprise Products at 6 to 7 percent and Williams at 3 percent, all above the S&P 500 yield.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A concrete high-yield basket to screen against, concentrated in midstream energy and financials rather than traditional defensives.

insights.claim: Skousen deliberately avoids double-digit dividend yields because those companies are likely to cut their payouts in a crisis.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A practical yield ceiling for income screens: treat double-digit yields as a distress signal, not an opportunity.

insights.claim: Skousen argues a stock that raises its dividend during a correction should be held rather than sold, because that behavior signals it will recover.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Gives a fundamental hold-versus-sell rule during drawdowns that is observable in real time via dividend declarations.

insights.claim: Skousen expresses commodity views through equities rather than the commodities themselves, preferring miners and royalty companies such as Franco Nevada over holding metal, though he still recommends physical gold and silver coins despite theft and storage risk.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Royalty companies offer commodity upside with lower operational beta than miners, whose early-stage production exposure makes their beta quite high.

insights.claim: Skousen holds Southern Copper as a copper play with copper at an all-time high, explicitly tying the metal to data center and infrastructure buildout.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Copper equities are a second-derivative AI trade with a commodity floor, less exposed to model-obsolescence risk than semiconductor names.

insights.claim: Skousen prefers uranium and small modular nuclear plants over wind and solar, which he calls extremely expensive, and notes uranium prices are rising.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Positions uranium as the multi-year energy answer for data centers, with the caveat that build timelines run into years.

insights.claim: Skousen expects elevated oil and gas prices to persist because data centers need oil and gas for energy until nuclear plants can take over, which takes years, and he treats oil as a shorter-term trade tied to the Middle East war ending.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Defines a clear exit condition for the energy trade: sell when the war ends and prices fall, but the structural data center demand extends the runway.
insights.quote: you need oil and gas to fund the energy needs of the data centers

insights.claim: Skousen gets Bitcoin exposure through BLOK, an ETF of blockchain and crypto companies, rather than owning Bitcoin directly, arguing the equities are a leveraged way to profit and have outperformed Bitcoin itself.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: An operating-leverage route to crypto beta; worth comparing crypto-equity basket returns against spot before choosing an expression.

insights.claim: Skousen holds Amgen as his favorite Dow stock on the thesis that drug industry innovation pays off over time, while warning that FDA approval stages require patience.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A long-duration, non-AI diversifier whose drawdowns can offset commodity gains on any given day, as he illustrated with copper up 8% and Amgen down 8%.

insights.claim: Skousen targets a portfolio beta only slightly above 1 relative to the market despite holding volatile mining and speculative positions.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Quantifies how far the dividend sleeve offsets the speculative sleeve, a useful construction target for investors copying the approach.

themes.theme: AI capex risk, speculation sizing and IPO mechanics

insights.claim: Skousen says tech stocks could fall in half and still be overvalued, yet he still holds positions in them.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Reveals a trend-follower holding assets he believes are fundamentally overpriced, which makes the exit trigger, not the valuation, the thing to monitor.
insights.quote: tech stocks could fall in half and still be overvalued

insights.claim: Skousen warns a significant correction could hit before the billions Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and other tech companies are pouring into AI data centers actually pay off, since that capex is consuming huge amounts of their cash flow.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Frames the AI trade as a short-term cash flow loss for a long-term gain, so free cash flow compression is the metric that would break the rally.

insights.claim: Skousen says SpaceX and Tesla were subject to hyper-promotion and that SpaceX is currently losing money because of xAI, despite his having previously promoted routes into SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A caution on the highest-profile private AI-adjacent names: promotional intensity is running ahead of the underlying profitability.

insights.claim: Skousen would buy Anthropic or OpenAI only through pre-IPO private placements, arguing that once the IPO comes the insiders are selling and it becomes hard to make money.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Sets the rule for the coming AI IPO wave: access matters more than the name, and post-listing buyers are structurally disadvantaged.
insights.quote: Once the IPO comes out, I mean, that's when the insiders are starting to sell, and it's really hard to make money.

insights.claim: Skousen uses the 'burning match' metaphor for late-stage IPO distribution, where the match is passed along until someone gets burned, and says that someone tends to be the retail investor.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A mental model for sizing participation in hot listings: assume you are late in the chain unless you have pre-IPO access.
insights.quote: It's called the burning match. You know when you light a match you and then you pass it on well at some point somebody gets burned.

insights.claim: Skousen sees defense-linked small caps building drones and missiles as a strong way to play war and defense spending without owning Lockheed Martin.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Small-cap drone suppliers offer higher torque to defense budgets than the primes, at the cost of single-contract concentration risk.

insights.claim: Skousen's speculation rule is strict position sizing: never back up the truck on a story stock, because a small position can still make a lot of money and you will be glad it was small if the thesis fails.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Applies directly to loss-making AI names like CoreWeave: participate with convex, small allocations rather than concentrated bets.

insights.claim: Skousen highlights Main Street Capital (MAIN), a business development company yielding about 7 percent that invests in private pre-IPO companies, as the only stock paying both a monthly and a quarterly dividend, with only about 1 percent of its portfolio in default and returns of roughly 10 to 20 percent a year including dividends.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable income vehicle offering indirect private-company exposure, with his own stated expectation capped at 10 to 20 percent, not a multibagger.
insights.quote: It's the only stock that pays a monthly and quarterly dividend.

insights.claim: Skousen names Trump's tariff trade war and the ongoing Middle East war as the two policies actively negative for the market, saying tariffs unambiguously raise costs.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Two identifiable political risk vectors whose resolution or escalation would move margins and energy prices in opposite directions.
